{"task": {"id": "I_kwDOVaC1p88AAAABbmiKmg", "item_id": "PVTI_lAHOAHSLSM4BpEKozhFKHsU", "project_id": "PVT_kwHOAHSLSM4BpEKo", "number": 38, "title": "Reduce workspace clutter with contextual controls and progressive disclosure", "body": "## Problem

The new three-pane workspace from #36 has the right overall composition, but the page is still visually cluttered. The current `web/index.html` puts lengthy onboarding text, always-visible file-management controls, an initially expanded settings section, redundant headings and context-specific operating instructions directly into the primary work areas.

This conflicts with the existing [three UI/UX principles](https://github.com/takahirox/webrtl#uiux): **Keep it simple; Show, don't tell; Intuitive and predictable**.

Refine the *existing* layout rather than replacing it or adding a new design system.

## Changes requested

### 1. Make the project sidebar about navigation (highest priority)
- Keep top module and the actual project file list prominent.
- Replace the permanently visible filename input and Add/Rename/Remove buttons with compact, discoverable file actions (e.g. Add/Import icons with accessible names, contextual Rename/Remove).
- Preserve all existing operations, keyboard access, and clear confirmation for destructive removal or example replacement where necessary.
- Collapse **Project settings** initially; keep output interface and HDL frontend easy to locate, and reveal their implications near the relevant controls.
- Move the always-visible “First Compile loads ~185 MB of tools…” paragraph into contextual **first-compile** feedback, without concealing a meaningful download/memory warning before the user starts it.
- Keep source limits/storage/help accessible in secondary disclosures rather than repeating instructional paragraphs in the main sidebar.

### 2. Simplify example loading and header
- Present example selection/loading as one coherent, predictable workflow rather than an awkward prominent selector + long “Load example (replaces project)” button.
- Make replacement behavior explicit at the point of action; avoid accidental loss of edited in-memory files. Do not silently replace a project just because a selector changes.
- Keep Compile, Run, Pause, Step, Reset, Fast/Debug and status discoverable without a large wall of labels or redundant headings.

### 3. Make simulation output the focus
- In **Fast** mode, emphasize the actual board output (counter value, generic I/O, video canvas, audio status) and concise runtime state, not explanatory prose.
- In **Debug** mode, expose actual hierarchical signal/RAM inspection, input controls, supported signal condition and sampled history. Preserve state when switching Fast→Pause→Debug→Fast.
- Condense the persistent SNES keyboard/controller help and detailed experimental notes into a discoverable contextual help area. Keep cartridge loading, controller focus guidance and legal ROM warning usable.
- Replace persistent “Step = one full clock cycle. Run = 10 cycles per second.” and similar paragraphs with concise contextual hints or tooltips where useful. Do not misstate actual run speed.

### 4. Make details and errors contextual
- Keep the diagnostics/detail pane compact or collapsed when there is nothing important to show; surface compilation errors automatically and accessibly when they occur.
- Remove redundant headings such as “Editor”, “Simulation” and “Diagnostics & details” *where pane location and control labels already communicate purpose*. Preserve semantic landmarks and accessible names even if visual headings are reduced.
- Keep compiler diagnostics, CPU trace and selected-signal history reachable without scattering duplicated controls across multiple panes.

### 5. Preserve the responsive three-pane workspace
- At wide viewport, left = project files, center = editing, right = actual output; bottom = optional diagnostics.
- At narrow viewport, keep core actions visible and prevent unreadable columns or horizontal page overflow.
- Avoid new frameworks, unsupported fake IDE capabilities, SNES-specific assumptions or unrelated RTL/runtime changes.

## Pre-merge acceptance criteria

- [ ] The default freshly opened browser workspace no longer shows the 185 MB explanation, file-name CRUD form, expanded project settings and lengthy help paragraphs simultaneously. A user can identify the file, editor and Compile/Run workflow without reading onboarding prose.
- [ ] All existing file Add/Import/Rename/Remove and example-loading operations remain functional; tests cover edited file retention, safe replacement/removal, keyboard focus and accessible control names.
- [ ] The first compile still communicates the actual toolchain download/memory implications before or at initiation, with truthful progress and failure handling; no mandatory human confirmation unless required for meaningful consent.
- [ ] Fast and Debug show only their relevant controls while preserving generic RTL inspection, break conditions, bounded signal history and lossless pause/resume.
- [ ] Board-specific SNES cartridge/controller, Canvas/video, audio and generic I/O behavior remain available and functional, with contextual rather than always-expanded instructions.
- [ ] Diagnostics remain discoverable, and errors become immediately visible and announced without forcing the user to hunt through collapsed panels.
- [ ] Representative desktop and narrow viewport automated browser checks validate reduced default clutter, essential actions, responsive layout and no accidental feature loss. Use focused checks and the repository's Fast PR CI rather than an unrelated full 260-cartridge rerun.
- [ ] Existing README UI/UX principles remain canonical; update only relevant UI help/documentation and do not add a competing principles document.

## Verification

Use the existing HTML/CSS/JS and browser tests. Prefer objective DOM/visibility/focus and interaction assertions. A subjective human-only approval gate is not required. Any necessary public GitHub Pages check of the deployed layout belongs **after** merge, not to pre-merge acceptance.

## Related

- #24 — UI/UX principles
- #36 — responsive three-pane layout
- #32 — Fast/Debug mode and state preservation
- #34 — bounded Fast PR CI
